      Help
      
      
      What does each option do? Quick answers below. Open the full README for deeper detail.
      
    
      

    
      
      
      
      
    
      

    
    
      
      
      30-second overview
      
      
      
        Sovereign turns any file (or text) into a string of letters and digits you can write down,
        print, or tattoo. Optionally encrypt with a password. Optionally save metadata to a
        key record so you can recover the file later without remembering every detail.
      
      
      
        
        
      1. Pick an alphabet (which characters end up in the output). b32 is the safe default for tattoos.
        2. 
        
      2. Pick an encryption mode (None / Key Vault / Salted / No-salt).
        3. 
        
      3. Pick a header tier (how much metadata to embed in the output).
        4. 
        
      4. Encode. Back up the key record if you used Key Vault.
        5. 
      
      
    
      

    
    
      
      
      Encryption modes
      
      
      
        
      ModeOutput overheadWhat it's for
      
        
          
      
            None
            0 bytes
            No password. Anyone with the encoded string can decode. Use for non-sensitive archival.
          
      
          
      
            Key Vault
            0 bytes
            AES-256 with salt & IV stored in a key record (not in the output). Smallest encrypted string. Requires the key record file to decode. Best for tattoos.
          
      
          
      
            Salted
            +16 bytes (~20–26 chars)
            Standard OpenSSL mode. Encoded string is fully self-contained — anyone with the password can decode. Portable.
          
      
          
      
            No-salt
            0 bytes
            Deterministic AES-256: same input + password always produce the same output. Vulnerable to rainbow tables for weak passwords. Power-user option.
          
      
              
      
      
    
      

    
    
      
      
      Header tiers
      
      
      The header is a small prefix on the encoded string that tells the decoder what to do.
        More metadata = easier recovery decades later, but more characters on your skin.
      
      
      
        
      TierLooks likeExtra charsTrade-off
      
        
          
      
            Bare
            JBSWY3DPEB...
            0
            Smallest output. You must remember (or store separately) the alphabet used.
          
      
          
      
            Key ref
            KV|a3f2b1c8|JBSWY...
            12
            Embeds an 8-char ID that links to your key record. Decoder finds everything else automatically. Only useful when you have the key record.
          
      
          
      
            Full SV1
            SV1|fp:dab1d0de|b:32|JBSWY...
            ~22
            Self-describing — anyone can decode without your key record (still needs password for encrypted data). Most portable, longest output.
          
      
              
      
      
      
      
        Header tier and Encryption mode are independent — you can combine any header with any encryption.
        Common combinations:
      
      
      
        
        
      • Tattoo, max security: Bare + Key Vault (need key record & password)
        • 
        
      • Tattoo, auto-decode: Key ref + Key Vault (need key record & password)
        • 
        
      • Portable encrypted archive: Full SV1 + Salted (need only password)
        • 
        
      • Plain backup: Full SV1 + None (open with anyone)
        • 
      
      
    
      

    
    
      
      
      Fingerprint size (Full SV1 only)
      
      
      When using the Full SV1 header, the fingerprint identifies which alphabet was used.
        More characters = unambiguous identification, fewer = shorter output.
      
      
      
        
      SizeHeader looks likeExtra charsTrade-off
      
        
          
      
            Full (8)
            SV1|fp:dab1d0de|b:32|
            ~22
            Unambiguous: 4 billion combinations. Always pick the right alphabet on decode. Default.
          
      
          
      
            Short (2)
            SV1|fp:da|b:32|
            ~16
            256 combinations. 1-in-256 chance of two alphabets sharing the same prefix. Saves 6 characters.
          
      
          
      
            None (0)
            SV1|b:32|
            ~9
            Base number only. Decoder must guess between alphabets with the same base. Saves 12 characters.
          
      
              
      
      
    
      

    
    
      
      
      About Key Vault mode
      
      
      Key Vault is a custom AES-256-CBC mode that puts everything except your password
        in a separate file (sv_key_records.json). The encoded string itself is just
        ciphertext bytes turned into letters — no salt prefix, no header required.
      
      
      You need three things to decode:
      
      
        
        
      1. The encoded string (the tattoo)
        2. 
        
      2. The key record (the JSON file or its printed card)
        3. 
        
      3. Your password
        4. 
      
      
      
      Why use it? Shortest possible encrypted output. Salted mode adds ~20 chars
        of Salted__ prefix to every encode; Key Vault adds zero.
      
      
      What to back up: Export each key record from the Vault tab. The exporter
        writes a .txt recovery card AND a recovery.html that works
        offline in any browser — it derives the AES key from your password using the browser's
        built-in PBKDF2, then prints the exact OpenSSL command.
      
      
      The trade-off: If you lose all copies of the key record, even your password
        cannot recover the data. Salt and IV are unique per encode — they cannot be regenerated.
        Key Vault treats the record as essential key material.
      
    
      

    
    
      
      
      Compression
      
      
      Compression shrinks the data before encryption (compressed ciphertext doesn't compress).
        Sovereign uses raw-mode compression that strips all algorithm headers from the stream —
        the algorithm name lives in a tiny CV1|c:X| prefix on the encoded string, or in the key record.
      
      
      
        
      ModeBest forNotes
      
        
          
      
            None
            Pre-compressed or random data
            No CV1 prefix. Use when input won't compress (images, encrypted files, random bytes).
          
      
          
      
            Auto
            Anything unknown
            Tries Deflate, LZMA (and LPAQ if available), picks the smallest. Falls back to None if nothing helps.
          
      
          
      
            Deflate
            Short text (~30–200 chars)
            zlib raw deflate. Python stdlib, fast. Often best for tiny inputs because LZMA carries a small overhead.
          
      
          
      
            LZMA
            Longer text (~150+ chars)
            Python stdlib LZMA2 preset 9 + EXTREME. Usually 5–15% denser than Deflate on natural-language text.
          
      
          
      
            LPAQ
            Maximum compression on short English text
            External binary (set its path in Settings). Sovereign auto-finds lpaq8.exe inside a PEAzip install. Disabled if not configured.
          
      
              
      
      
      
      
        Compression pairs with every encryption mode. The CV1 prefix adds 6 characters — usually a net win
        for inputs that compress at all. Tiny strings that inflate under compression are handled by Auto
        which simply picks "None".
      
      
    
      

    
    
      
      
      Alphabets — what to choose
      
      
        
        
      • b32 — 32 characters: A–Z + 2–7. Uppercase only, no ambiguous shapes. Default for tattoos. Legible as ink fades.
        • 
        
      • b37 — 37 unambiguous characters, no 0/O or 1/I. Best legibility on aged skin.
        • 
        
      • hex — 0–9 + A–F. Decodable by hand with a pencil and paper. Longest output.
        • 
        
      • b64 / b85 — densest, but uses mixed case and special characters not ideal for skin.
        • 
        
      • Custom — design your own alphabet in the Editor tab.
        • 
      
      
    
      

    
    
      
      
      Recovery: what to back up
      
      
      
        
      Mode you usedWhat you need to keep
      
        
          
      
            None / Full SV1
            Nothing — the encoded string is fully self-contained.
          
      
          
      
            Salted with built-in alphabet
            Just your password. Sovereign or any decoder can recover the rest.
          
      
          
      
            Custom alphabet
            Export the alphabet's key card (Library tab) and store with medical/estate records.
          
      
          
      
            Key Vault
            Export each key record (Vault tab). Includes recovery.html. Without the record, the data is unrecoverable.
          
      
              
      
      
    
      

    
    
      
      
      If this app no longer exists
      
      
      Sovereign is designed so your data survives the loss of the app itself:
      
      
        
        
      • Built-in alphabets (hex, b32, b64) can be decoded by any base-N tool. The character order is public.
        • 
        
      • Custom alphabets: the key card lists every character in order — sufficient to rebuild.
        • 
        
      • Key Vault: recovery.html generated on export does the PBKDF2 key derivation in any web browser, then prints a standard OpenSSL command.
        • 
        
      • OpenSSL itself is open-source and likely to exist for decades.
        •
